idiom_name: data class Pizza(val size: String, val cheese: Int = 0) + named arguments + copy()
implementation_notes: Kotlin's default and named arguments remove the builder's reason to exist: callers pass only the parameters they care about by name (Pizza(size = "L", olives = 3)), the primary constructor is the single construction path, and data class adds copy() so producing a variant of an existing value is one call; apply { } configures a mutable object that already carries defaults. Kotlin's own literature recommends this over the classic builder, reserving a type-safe DSL builder for products whose structure is hierarchical (see the DSL variant).
code_sketch:
data class Pizza(val size: String, val cheese: Int = 0,
                 val olives: Int = 0, val bacon: Int = 0)

val lunch = Pizza(size = "L", olives = 3)          // named + defaulted
val vegan = lunch.copy(cheese = 0, bacon = 0)      // variant of an instance

class Client { var timeoutMs: Int = 1_000 }
val client = Client().apply { timeoutMs = 5_000 }  // configure in place
pitfalls: Named arguments bind by name at compile time, so renaming a constructor parameter breaks every call site, while a builder method can be renamed behind the scenes.
A public total constructor has nowhere to validate combinations: rules spanning parameters belong in an init { require(...) } block, which throws rather than returning an error.
var properties with defaults invite post-construction mutation; keep the class immutable (val) unless the object is genuinely stateful.

variants.name: Type-safe DSL builder (lambda with receiver + @DslMarker)
variants.idiom_name: fun html(init: HTML.() -> Unit): HTML with @DslMarker-annotated receivers
variants.implementation_notes: For nested products Kotlin prefers a DSL over a fluent chain: a top-level function takes a lambda with receiver, creates the builder, runs the block and returns the accumulated value (fun table(init: TableBuilder.() -> Unit) = TableBuilder().apply(init)), and @DslMarker on the shared receiver type stops an inner scope from calling the outer receiver's members and nesting an element in the wrong parent. The builder classes stay private to the DSL and there is no separate terminal build() step, because the function that runs the lambda is the terminal step.
pitfalls: Without @DslMarker on the common receiver supertype both receivers stay in scope and a nested element can be added to the wrong parent without a compiler error.
A DSL that mutates and returns the same instance gives no immutability: copy the result before publishing it, or hand out an immutable view.
